newsitem.title: USA: Dow slips after first rise above 7,300 points.
newsitem.headline: Dow slips after first rise above 7,300 points.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks were lower Tuesday as profit-taking spoiled a bid by the Dow Jones industrial average's to close above the 7,300-point level for the first time.
The Dow closed down 18.54 points at 7,274.21 after a rally to 7,315.83 briefly beat out Monday's record close of 7,292.75.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,325 to 1,135 on active volume of 489 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The selling also stemmed from a report that the Federal Reserve is likely to raise short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point at its policy-setting meeting next week.
"There is a very good chance the Fed will do another 25 basis points (one-quarter percentage point), and virtually no chance it will do 50 basis points," one source at the Fed told Reuters.
The Federal Open Market Committee raised the funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent in March in an effort to ward off inflation.

"I'm impressed -- we've got multiple excuses to pull out the rug from under the Dow. It's acting very well considering the circumstances," said Alfred Goldman, chief market analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons.
The last increase in interest rates set the stage for a selloff that wiped out nearly 700 points from the blue-chip Dow index.
"They could easily justify one more rate hike but not a series of rate hikes. We still don't see the whites of inflation's eyes yet," said Anthony Chan, chief economist for Banc One.
Chan said considering the headstrong gains made by the market in the past few weeks, he did not believe that stocks have fully anticipated the possibility of a rate increase.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell nearly half a point, raising its yield to 6.93 percent from Monday's 6.89 percent. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.
Wall Street cleared the first of three major economic data hurdles unscathed Tuesday when a report on retail sales for April came in generally as expected.
Retail sales fell 0.3 percent, but the market-friendly data caused little reaction in either the stock or bond markets.

On Wednesday, the government will issue its Producer Price Index report for April and the next day, the Consumer Price Index, although economists say the data should not contain any inflationary signals that could scare Wall Street.
The Dow exhibited some of its recent trademark volatility, lurching down 50 points late in the session, but the index recovered much of that by the final bell.
Some profit-taking in the 30 stock blue-chip index was masked by strength in International Business Machines Corp.
IBM hit an all-time high of 177-1/8 before settling with a gain of 1-3/4 at 173-5/8. Big Blue's strength was ignited by news that Goldman Sachs had added the stock to its recommended list.
Intel Corp., the world's biggest chipmaker, fell 6-3/4 to 152-3/8 after rival Digital Equipment Corp. filed a patent infringment suit against Intel and said it would seek a "huge" damage award.
Digital closed up 2-1/8 to 35-1/4.
General Motors Corp. lost 1-3/8 to 56-7/8 after 8,200 union workers in Ohio walked off their jobs, threatening a broad shutdown of GM's North American vehicle operations.
The Nasdaq Composite index lost 10.60 points to 1,333.59.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was off 4.53 at 833.13. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.13 to 579.60.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.60 to 433.97. The average share was down 15 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,849.216 down 36.659 or 0.46 percent.
